questions.q: A coach says 'Watch the next bird.' What will you see?

options.text: A live pigeon released from a box
A clay target thrown by a trap
A bird-shaped paper target on a board
A drone

questions.explain: 'Bird' is shooters' slang for a clay target; the FITASC rules forbid shooting at live animals.

questions.q: What does a shotgun fire?

options.text: One single bullet
A small arrow-like dart
A cloud of small pellets (shot)
A ball filled with paint

questions.explain: The shot leaves the muzzle as a small cloud of pellets, so the shooter points ahead of the moving target.

questions.q: Which statement about Compak® Sporting is correct?

options.text: A compact version on one field, stations in a line
It is a course of stands spread through a forest
It is shot only at live game birds in the field
It uses a single trap and a single station

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting brings Sporting™-style targets onto one small field with five stations and six traps.

questions.q: What do you shoot at in clay shooting?

options.text: Live birds released from a box
Clay targets thrown by a trap
Paper targets fixed on a board

questions.explain: You shoot only at artificial targets thrown by a trap. Shooting at live animals is forbidden.

questions.q: What is a trap?

options.text: A shotgun with a short barrel
The referee who runs the stand
A machine that throws targets

questions.explain: A trap is the machine that throws a target into the air or rolls it along the ground.

questions.q: Why does a shooter point the gun ahead of a moving target?

options.text: The shot needs time to reach the target
The referee asks all shooters to do it
It keeps the gun from touching the target

questions.explain: The target moves and the shot takes time to get there, so the gun points where the target will be a moment later.

questions.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give?
questions.explain: Each layout gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more).

questions.q: How many traps are there on one Compak field?

options.text: Six, lettered A to F
Four, lettered A to D
Ten, two at each station

questions.explain: A Compak® Sporting field has 6 traps lettered A to F and 5 shooting stations in a line.

questions.q: In which discipline do you walk a course from stand to stand?

options.text: Compak® Sporting
Both, in the same way
Sporting™

questions.explain: In Sporting™ you move from stand to stand over natural ground; in Compak® Sporting you stay on one field and move one station to the right.

questions.q: Your first shot misses a single target. What does the rule allow?

options.text: The referee repeats the target
You must open the gun at once
You may fire the second barrel

questions.explain: In Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a single target must allow two shots, so a miss with the first can still be followed by the second.

questions.q: How big is a Sporting™ shooting stand?

options.text: A 1 m square or a 1 m circle
A 3 m square with a fence
Any size the club likes

questions.explain: The rules set a 1 m square or a circle 1 m across.

questions.q: What does the target menu show?

options.text: The prices in the café
The traps in shooting order
The scores of the squad

questions.explain: The menu in front of the stand lists the traps in shooting order and any special targets.

questions.q: Which target rolls along the ground?

options.text: Battue
Midi
Rabbit

questions.explain: The rabbit target rolls along the ground and bounces over bumps.

questions.q: What is the frame at each Compak® Sporting station for?

options.text: It holds the target menu
It limits the swing of the gun
It marks where spectators stand

questions.explain: The firing angle limiter stops the gun pointing in an unsafe direction and keeps the shooter inside the station.

questions.q: Which first step does this lesson suggest?

options.text: Buy a gun and practise alone
A taster lesson with a coach
Watch videos, then enter a championship

questions.explain: A coach teaches safety and good basics from the very start.

questions.q: Does a beginner need their own gun?

options.text: Yes, grounds do not lend guns
Yes, and it must be a pump-action
No, many grounds hire guns out

questions.explain: Many grounds have club guns you can shoot under supervision; the rules depend on national law.

questions.q: Which gun is NOT allowed in FITASC competitions?

options.text: A pump-action gun
A 12-gauge over-and-under
A semi-automatic

questions.explain: Pump-action guns are not allowed. A semi-automatic is allowed, but it may be loaded with two cartridges at most.

questions.q: Which of these is a regular cost?

options.text: Your own gun
Cartridges and targets
A gun safe

questions.explain: Cartridges and targets are used up at each session.

questions.q: How many cartridges should you take for a round of 25 targets?

options.text: At least 25, plus spares
10, the ground adds more
Exactly 25, no spares

questions.explain: You need one cartridge per target, and you may fire a second shot at a single target, so take spares.

questions.q: How does a beginner usually start?

options.text: Buys an expensive gun first
Enters a championship abroad
A taster session with a coach

questions.explain: A taster session with a hired gun lets you try the sport without big spending.

questions.q: When do you usually need a European Firearms Pass?

options.text: For a lesson at your local ground
When you hire a gun abroad
Taking your own gun across the EU

questions.explain: The pass is issued by the EU country where you live, for travelling with your own guns. Without it, you can hire a gun at the destination.

questions.q: Where may you load the gun?

options.text: Anywhere at the ground, if the gun points at the ground
Only on the stand, pointing down the range, once shooting is allowed
On the way to the stand, so you are ready when called

questions.explain: Cartridges go in only on the stand, with the gun pointing down the range, after the referee or instructor allows shooting.

questions.q: What must you do before turning round on the stand?

options.text: Open the gun and take out all cartridges, fired or not
Put the safety catch on and keep the gun closed
Take out only the unfired cartridges, then close the gun

questions.explain: You turn round only with the gun open and empty; a safety catch is no substitute for an open gun.

questions.q: The gun clicks but does not fire. What should the shooter do?

options.text: Open it at once to see what went wrong
Turn round and show the gun to the coach
Stay put, gun down the range, and wait for the referee
Put the safety on and call for the target again

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the shooter to stay put until the referee inspects; opening or touching the safety first scores zero.

questions.q: How many cartridges may a semi-automatic hold?

options.text: One only
As many as the magazine takes
No more than two

questions.explain: In both disciplines a semi-automatic may hold no more than two cartridges.

questions.q: How is a semi-automatic carried between stands?

options.text: Closed, with the safety catch on
With the action open, muzzle up or down
On a sling over the shoulder, unloaded
With one cartridge in, safety on

questions.explain: Guns are carried open, semi-automatics with the action open, muzzles straight up or down; slings are not allowed.

questions.q: Someone shouts “Cease fire!”. What is the interpreter’s first job?

options.text: Repeat “Stop!” loudly and check that the guns are open
Explain to the guests why shooting has stopped
Ask the coach quietly what has happened
Wait until a guest asks what is going on

questions.explain: An emergency stop is repeated at once; explanations come only when all guns are open.

questions.q: Lightning is close and the referee has paused shooting. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the gun closed and wait on the stand
Open and unload the gun, then shelter in a building
Shelter under the nearest tall tree with your gun

questions.explain: During any pause the gun is open and empty, and in lightning you leave the open ground for a building.

questions.q: Who must wear hearing protection at a competition?

options.text: Only the shooter who is on the stand
Shooters and referees, but not spectators
Everyone near the layout, spectators too

questions.explain: The rules of both disciplines name shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: Your shooter walks onto the stand without safety glasses. How do the rules treat him?

options.text: He gets a warning and may shoot
He may shoot if the coach agrees
He loses one target
He is treated as absent

questions.explain: In both disciplines a shooter without eye or ear protection on the stand is treated as absent and may not shoot.

questions.q: Which gives the most hearing protection when many shots are fired?

options.text: Earplugs and ear muffs worn together
Electronic muffs with the volume turned up
Earplugs pushed in loosely, for comfort

questions.explain: Plugs and muffs together protect most, as long as both fit well.

questions.q: What is the advantage of electronic ear muffs?

options.text: They make safety glasses unnecessary
They soften the shot but let voices through
They block all sound, voices included

questions.explain: You are protected from the bang and still hear the referee’s commands.

questions.q: Which shorts are allowed at a FITASC competition?

options.text: Any sports shorts, as long as the shirt has sleeves
Bermuda-style shorts, ending no more than 5 cm above the knee
Short shorts in Compak® Sporting, but not in Sporting™
No shorts of any length, in either discipline

questions.explain: Short shorts are banned in both disciplines; long Bermuda-style shorts are accepted.

questions.q: Why are electronic ear muffs a good choice for an interpreter?

options.text: They soften the shot but let voices through
They are not required for interpreters
They block all sound completely
They record the coach

questions.explain: Hearing protection is compulsory near a layout, and electronic muffs let you hear the coach and referee.

questions.q: How do you carry a gun between stands?

options.text: Closed, on the shoulder, with the safety catch on
On a sling across the back, unloaded
Open, with the muzzle straight up or down

questions.explain: The gun is carried open, muzzle up or down; slings are not allowed in either discipline.

questions.q: Where does a gun go when you are not using it?

options.text: Upright in a gun rack or another place provided
Leaning against the car, closed and unloaded
Lying flat on the ground next to the stand

questions.explain: Guns stand upright in a gun rack or another place the ground provides, so they cannot fall; a semi-automatic stands with its action open.

questions.q: Where may you test-fire a gun?

options.text: On the first competition stand, before the round
On the test stand, if the ground has one
In a quiet corner of the car park

questions.explain: Test shots belong on the test stand; firing them on a competition stand is forbidden.

questions.q: What is mock shooting?

options.text: Shooting at a real target with a light practice cartridge
Calling for a target without any cartridge in the gun
Shouldering the gun and swinging it along an imagined target

questions.explain: Mock shooting means mounting the gun and swinging as if at a target. In Sporting™ it is not allowed anywhere at the ground, even on the stand before you call. In Compak® Sporting it is not allowed outside the shooting positions or while another squad member shoots.

questions.q: When may you step onto the stand?

options.text: As soon as the previous shooter has fired his last shot
When the stand is free and it is your turn
Together with the shooter before you, to save time

questions.explain: You step up only once the previous shooter has left the stand and it is your turn.

questions.q: May a friend give a shooter advice during a competition?

options.text: Yes, if he whispers it between targets
Only if the friend is a qualified coach
No: it counts as coaching and is penalised

questions.explain: Coaching during a competition is forbidden for everyone, coaches included: the shooter gets a yellow card.

questions.q: A loud phone call behind the stand clearly disturbs the shooter at the moment of the shot. What may the referee decide?

options.text: No Bird: the target is thrown again
Zero for the shooter
Nothing, phones are not in the rules
Yellow card for the shooter

questions.explain: If the referee sees the shooter was clearly disturbed, the target is a No Bird.

questions.q: How long do you have to call for a target in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: Up to 30 seconds
Up to 10 seconds
As long as you need

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting a shooter has at most 10 seconds; the first breach is a warning, a repeat in the same round is penalised.

questions.q: Where does the interpreter stand while the guest is shooting?

options.text: Beside the shooter, to see his face
In front of the stand, to see the target
Behind the stand, out of any line of the barrels
Wherever the referee cannot see

questions.explain: Everyone who is not shooting waits behind the stand, cage or F.A.L.; beside or in front of the stand you are in or near the swing of the barrels.

questions.q: When is the right moment to pass on the coach’s comment?

options.text: While the shooter is calling for the target
Between the call and the shot, in a whisper
As soon as the coach has finished speaking
Once the gun is open after a target or pair

questions.explain: The shooter’s routine must not be interrupted; speak only once the gun is open.

questions.q: What should a beginner buy first?

options.text: An expensive gun of their own
Their own eye and ear protection
A full set of coloured lenses
A large cartridge bag

questions.explain: Protection is needed from the first shot, and your own is more comfortable and hygienic.

questions.q: When is it sensible to buy a gun?

options.text: After some lessons and a fitting
Before the very first lesson
On the first day at the ground
Whenever a shop has a good sale

questions.explain: The coach helps choose a model and dimensions, and the law tells you which licences you need.

questions.q: Which vest works for both disciplines?

options.text: A vest with no pockets at all
A thick winter jumper instead
A vest with the 25 cm jacket line
Any vest, as long as it is bright

questions.explain: The line is needed in Sporting™ and does no harm in Compak® Sporting.

questions.q: A coach says 'Raise the comb'. Which part does he mean?

options.text: The top of the stock, where the cheek rests
The small bead at the end of the rib
The guard around the trigger
The choke tube at the muzzle

questions.explain: The comb is the top of the stock; raising it lifts the eye above the rib.

questions.q: What must a gun with a release trigger carry?

options.text: A red-painted barrel to warn others
A large 'R' sticker on the stock
A second, separate safety catch
Nothing: no marking is required

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require the 'R' warning sticker, on a fluorescent background, on the outer side of the buttstock.

questions.q: What is the barrel selector for?

options.text: To take the barrels off the action
To change the choke in the barrel
To throw the fired cases out
To choose which barrel fires first

questions.explain: The selector, often combined with the safety, sets the order of the barrels.

questions.q: What do the ejectors do when you open the gun?

options.text: They throw out the fired cases
They lock the barrels to the action
They set which barrel fires first
They soften the recoil of the shot

questions.explain: Ejectors throw out fired cases; simpler extractors only lift them a little.

questions.q: Which part do you take off first to remove the barrels?

options.text: The comb
The fore-end
The rib
The bead

questions.explain: The fore-end holds the barrels on the action; once it is off, the barrels come off.

questions.q: What does a coach mean by 'Break your gun'?

options.text: Damage the gun on purpose
Take the gun apart into pieces
Open the gun on its hinge
Clean the barrels of the gun

questions.explain: On a shooting ground 'break' means opening the gun on its hinge so it cannot fire.

questions.q: What size is a mini target usually?

options.text: 90 mm
About 60 mm
About 110 mm

questions.explain: A mini is usually 60 mm and a midi 90 mm. Names of small targets vary, so go by the millimetres on the menu.

questions.q: On a Sporting™ stand, a trap throws a midi instead of the standard shown on the menu. What happens?

options.text: No Bird, the target is repeated
It counts as a hit
The shooter loses the target
The round is cancelled

questions.explain: In Sporting™ a target of the wrong colour, size or type is a No Bird (it does not count) and is thrown again.

questions.q: Which target rolls along the ground?

options.text: Midi
Battue
Rabbit
Flash

questions.explain: The rabbit has a thick rim and is thrown on its edge along the ground.

questions.q: The menu says '70 mm'. The coach calls it a mini. What should you translate?

options.text: Correct it to 60 mm, since a mini is 60 mm
Keep the coach's word and the 70 mm on the menu
Call it a midi, since it is over 60 mm
Ask the coach to say 'super mini' instead

questions.explain: The rules name 70 mm and 60 mm sizes and the name 'super mini'; trust the millimetres on the menu and do not correct the coach.

questions.q: Which target flies edge-on, then turns to show its face and drops?

options.text: Battue
Midi
Rabbit

questions.explain: The battue is flat and thin: it flies edge-on, then turns and drops quickly.

questions.q: Which target leaves a cloud of coloured powder when it is hit?

options.text: ZZ target
Rocket
Flash target

questions.explain: A flash target is filled with coloured powder. It is scored like any other target.

questions.q: Which presentation usually needs the most lead?

options.text: A target going straight away
An incomer flying straight at the shooter
A crosser at the same distance
A rabbit rolling straight away

questions.explain: All of a crosser's speed is sideways, so you shoot furthest in front of it; targets flying straight away from you or towards you need little sideways lead.

questions.q: A target comes towards the shooter at an angle and passes to the side. What is it called?

options.text: Going-away
Quartering towards
Teal
Rafale

questions.explain: Quartering towards (or quartering in) is an angled target coming in; quartering away is the angled target moving off.

questions.q: Why should a target be read from the exact stand you will shoot from?

options.text: One trap can give a different angle from each stand
The rules forbid watching from any other place
Targets change colour from one stand to the next
Only the referee may stand anywhere else

questions.explain: The angle between the shooter and the target's line changes with the position, so the presentation changes too.

questions.q: A crosser flies far from you. Compared with a near one at the same speed, it needs…

options.text: more lead
less lead
the same lead

questions.explain: The further the target, the further it travels while the shot is on its way, so it needs more lead.

questions.q: A crosser is slowing down at your break point. Compared with one at full speed, it needs…

options.text: more lead
less lead
no lead at all

questions.explain: A slower target moves less while the shot travels, so it needs less lead.

questions.q: From whose point of view are “left” and “right” given for a crosser?

options.text: The shooter's
The referee's
The trapper's

questions.explain: Directions are the shooter's: an L→R crosser flies from the shooter's left to right.

questions.q: The coach says “long crosser”. What does “long” mean?

options.text: The target is far away
The target flies for a long time
The target is a long, oval clay
The shooter should wait a long time

questions.explain: In coaching “long” describes distance. A long crosser is a far crosser, which needs more lead.

questions.q: What is true of crossers in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: Crossers are not allowed on a Compak
Only right-to-left crossers are allowed
Crossers may only be thrown as rabbits
An L→R and an R→L crosser are compulsory

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules make three trajectories compulsory: an L→R crosser, an R→L crosser and a going-away target.

questions.q: How does the lead on a quartering target compare with a full crosser at the same distance and speed?

options.text: It is the same as the crosser
It is always zero
It is larger than the crosser
It is smaller, depending on the angle

questions.explain: Only the sideways part of the movement needs sideways lead, so the closer the target is to a straight line away from you or towards you, the smaller the lead.

questions.q: Where does the coach usually want the front foot to point?

options.text: At the trap
At the pick-up point
At the referee
At the break point

questions.explain: Feet set to the break point keep the body relaxed where the shot happens. If the feet face the trap, the body cannot turn far enough to reach the break point.

questions.q: What do the Sporting™ rules require of the feet before the call?

options.text: Both feet inside the stand
The front foot on the stand line
Feet together
No requirement at all

questions.explain: The ready-position rule asks for both feet inside the 1 m shooting stand before the shooter calls.

questions.q: A left-handed shooter. The coach says “Open your front foot”. Which foot is it?

options.text: The left one, whatever the hand
The right one: a left-hander's front foot
The back foot, nearer the trap
Both feet together

questions.explain: For a left-hander the front foot is the right one. Translating “front foot” as front, not as left, avoids the mistake.

questions.q: How does a right-handed shooter usually place the feet?

options.text: Left foot slightly forward
Right foot far forward
Feet together, heels touching

questions.explain: A right-hander puts the left foot slightly forward, a left-hander the right.

questions.q: Which point should your feet be set up for?

options.text: Where the trap is
The break point
Where the squad waits

questions.explain: Then your body turns easily to exactly where you will break the target.

questions.q: Where must the shooter’s feet be in Sporting™ before calling?

options.text: Anywhere near the stand
Both inside the shooting stand
One foot inside, one outside

questions.explain: The Sporting™ rules require both feet inside the shooting stand before the call.

questions.q: In Sporting™, until when must the stock stay below the vest line?

options.text: Until the shooter has called
Until the referee gives a nod
Until the target is out and visible
Until the first shot is fired

questions.explain: The ready position is held until the target has been released and can be seen; only then may the gun be mounted.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may a shooter call for the target with the gun already at the shoulder?

options.text: No: it earns a yellow card
Only for rabbits and other low targets
Only between the two targets of a double
Yes: the gun position at the call is free

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting has no low-gun rule: the gun may be mounted or not at the call, but each target is shot from the shoulder.

questions.q: Why do coaches insist on the cheek staying on the comb?

options.text: The eye works as the rear sight, so it must sit in one place
To reduce the noise reaching the ear
Because the rules of both disciplines require it
To hide the face from the referee

questions.explain: A shotgun has no rear sight: your eye does that job, so a lifted cheek sends the shot high.

questions.q: Which is right during the mount?

options.text: The face goes to the gun
The gun comes to the face
The head bends to the rib

questions.explain: The head stays level and the gun comes to the cheek and shoulder.

questions.q: How far below the shoulder axis is the vest line drawn in Sporting™?

options.text: 10 cm
25 cm
40 cm

questions.explain: The line is drawn 25 cm below the shoulder axis, parallel to it.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, may you call for the target with the gun already mounted?

options.text: Yes, the position at the call is free
No, only from a low gun position
Only on simultaneous doubles

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free; the low gun with a vest line is a Sporting™ rule.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left dominant eye. What is this called?

options.text: Central vision
Hard focus
Cross-dominance
Leading edge

questions.explain: Cross-dominance is a dominant eye on the opposite side to the shooting shoulder.

questions.q: Why is looking back at the bead to check the lead a fault?

options.text: It is forbidden by the rules of both disciplines
It usually slows or stops the gun, so the shot goes behind
The bead reflects the sun into the eye
It makes the target change colour in flight

questions.explain: When you look at the gun instead of the target, the swing tends to slow or stop. The target slips to the edge of your vision, and the shot goes behind.

questions.q: Where does the anti-dominance dot usually go?

options.text: On the safety glasses, in front of one eye
On the bead at the end of the rib
On the rib, halfway along it
On the vest line, below the shoulder

questions.explain: Safety glasses are compulsory anyway, so a small dot on the lens in front of the non-dominant eye is the simplest remedy.

questions.q: What does the hand-triangle test show?

options.text: Which eye is dominant
Whether the gun fits
How far the target flies

questions.explain: The eye that keeps the object in the triangle is the master eye.

questions.q: A right-handed shooter has a left master eye. What is it called?

options.text: Cross-dominance
A flinch
Follow-through

questions.explain: A master eye on the other side from the stock is cross-dominance.

questions.q: Who should help you decide how to shoot with cross-dominance?

options.text: Another squad member during a competition
A qualified coach
The referee on the stand

questions.explain: A coach will take into account your age, experience and how strong the dominance is. Besides, coaching during a competition is not allowed.

questions.q: Which point is about the eyes, not the gun?

options.text: Hold point
Break point
Pick-up point
Insertion point

questions.explain: The pick-up point is where the eyes first see the target clearly; the hold point is for the muzzles.

questions.q: What usually happens if the hold point is too close to the trap?

options.text: The referee calls No Bird
The gun has to chase the target
The gun has almost no room to move
The target slows down

questions.explain: Too near the trap, the target leaves at full speed past the muzzles, so the gun has to chase it. Too little room to move is the problem of a hold point too far out.

questions.q: In Sporting™, the shooter on the stand asks to see the presentation again. What is the maximum per target of the menu?

options.text: Two targets
None: no repeats are allowed
As many as the shooter wants
Exactly five

questions.explain: The referee will show it again if asked, but no more than twice per target on the menu.

questions.q: What is the hold point?

options.text: Where the barrels wait when you call
Where the cartridges are kept
Where the target lands

questions.explain: The hold point is where you hold the muzzles before calling.

questions.q: Where do your eyes go before calling?

options.text: On the barrels
To the pick-up point
On the target menu

questions.explain: Your eyes wait where the target first becomes clearly visible.

questions.q: Which point are your feet set for?

options.text: The pick-up point
The hold point
The break point

questions.explain: Feet are set for the break point, so the body is most comfortable there.

questions.q: What is perceived lead?

options.text: The real distance in front of the clay in the air
The gap the shooter sees between muzzle and target
The lead written on the target menu
The distance from the stand to the trap

questions.explain: Perceived lead is the picture at the muzzle; actual lead is the real distance in the air and is much larger.

questions.q: Of the methods with a moving gun, which usually gives the largest perceived lead?

options.text: Swing-through
Pull-away
Maintained lead
All are identical

questions.explain: With maintained lead the gun moves no faster than the target, so nothing is added on its own and you have to see the whole gap. With ambush, where the gun is still, the gap seen is even bigger.

questions.q: Which target needs almost no sideways lead?

options.text: A target going straight away
A long crosser
A quartering-away target at 45°
A crosser at 40 m

questions.explain: A straight going-away target has no sideways movement; any lead it needs is vertical.

questions.q: Why do you need lead?

options.text: So that shot and target meet
To reduce the recoil
To make the target fly slower

questions.explain: While the shot flies the target moves on, so you shoot in front of it.

questions.q: In which method do the barrels stay in front of the target throughout?

options.text: Swing-through
Maintained lead
Pull-away

questions.explain: Maintained lead: the barrels start in front and keep the gap.

questions.q: Which target needs the least lead?

options.text: A distant, fast crosser
A target going straight away
A high crossing target

questions.explain: A target going straight away or coming straight in hardly moves sideways relative to the barrels.

questions.q: With which method must the shooter see the biggest gap at the moment of decision?

options.text: Swing-through
Pull-away
Maintained lead
Ambush

questions.explain: With ambush the gun is still, and the target keeps moving during the reaction time. So the gap seen at the decision must be bigger than the actual lead.

questions.q: Why do many shooters begin with a coach rather than teach themselves?

options.text: Lessons with a coach cost less than shooting alone
A coach watches safety and catches faults before they set in
The rules do not allow shooting without a coach nearby

questions.explain: Faults are hard to feel from behind the gun, and a habit that has set in takes longer to change than to learn well from the start.

questions.q: What does a coach usually check at the first lesson?

options.text: Your ranking in national competitions
How many cartridges you can carry
Which of your eyes is the master eye

questions.explain: The master eye decides whether the gun points where you look. If your master eye is on the other side from the shoulder you shoot from (for example, left eye, right shoulder), the coach suggests a fix. Common fixes are closing one eye or putting a dot on your glasses.

questions.q: A trial lesson felt unclear and uncomfortable. What do many shooters do next?

options.text: Try a lesson with another coach
Give up clay shooting for good
Put up with it and change nothing

questions.explain: Coaches explain in different ways, and looking for one who suits you is normal.
